newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Fourth Australian rate cut seen less likely.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Fourth Australian rate cut seen less likely.

text.p: Australian interest rates are now unlikely to be cut a fourth time, unless there are signs of renewed weakness in economic activity over coming months, analysts said.
The winding back of expectations reflected signs of recovery in some parts of the economy, but the favourable low inflation outlook meant an easing was not totally off the agenda.
The median forecast of economists surveyed on Friday by Reuters was that a fourth rate cut was now a 30 percent chance, down from an even money bet two weeks ago.

A combination of higher than expected wages growth, signs of recovery in housing and employment, and some comments last week by Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Ian Macfarlane that the effects of the three cuts last year were starting to appear, was behind the winding back of expectations.

"Take a cautious RBA Governor, add a dash of solid economic activity data, and we have a reliable formula for producing interest rates on hold," Citibank Australia senior economist Annette Beacher said.
The official cash rate is currently 6.0 percent, after the RBA cut rates by a total of 150 basis points in three moves between July and December last year.

As well as stronger data, the RBA was seen waiting on the outcome of the union movement's 'living wage' claim in early March. The RBA has said the full claim would lead to a large increase in wages growth, and Macfarlane said last week it would be prudent to wait on the outcome of the case.
The Tuesday release of the RBA's quarterly economic report is seen confirming Macfarlane's comments, which were interpreted as suggesting rates were on hold.
"We expect the quarterly report to come close to suggesting cash rates are likely to stay unchanged for some time to come," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
In fact, there had been a de-facto easing of policy after a round of competition-induced mortgage rate cuts last week.
The Commonwealth Bank cut its rate by 70 basis points, closely followed by others, including National Australia Bank.

"The expectation is the other major banks will also match the mortage rate cuts," SBC Warburg chief economist Peter Horn said. "So I think that obviates the need for RBA to cut rates, even were they to think it necessary."
But while a rate cut was now seen as less likely, it was not out of the question, with the key seen as how activity-related data pans out over coming months.

"Given that the full impact of last year's cuts are yet to bear fruit, another easing of monetary policy might require a stalling of the recovery in housing and activity which now appears to be underway," ANZ Treasury economists said.
Inflation was seen well contained, and while wages data came in at the top end of expectations, the 3.9 percent annual growth rate was still in the RBA's 'comfort zone' for wages growth.

At the end of the month, the RBA will also receive updates on the pace of enterprise bargaining agreements. If those and the 'living wage' outcome were favourable, a cut could still be on the agenda despite emerging signs of stronger activity.
"If wages are not a threat, such signs of faster growth we have seen so far in 1997 do not seem to me to preclude a final easing," Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said.
The RBA had also not said another rate cut was off the agenda, just that it should give some time to see what impact the other three cuts were having.

"It's just that there is a need to sit back and assess what sort of momentum the rate cuts to date have imparted to the economy, and what this means for inflation and activity trajectories," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.
